titleText.es: Si soy un dios, ¿por qué Maru no es *mi* gato?
titleText.en: If I'm such a god, why isn't Maru *my* cat?
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute. The asterisks are part of both source strings.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, a procesador is the component that carries out instructions.

example.en: The processor runs the program.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: After a verb such as funcionar, a can introduce the speed or rate at which something operates.

example.es: La máquina funciona a cien ciclos por minuto.
example.en: The machine runs at one hundred cycles per minute.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Miles is the plural of mil when the number of thousands is not specified exactly.

example.en: Thousands of people arrived.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Millones is followed by de before the thing being counted.

example.en: There are millions of stars.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: A ciclo is one repeated round in a process or machine.

example.en: The motor completes several cycles.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: This noun names one second of time. It is separate from segundo meaning ‘second’ in an ordered list.

example.en: Wait one second.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, ejecutar means making a program or set of instructions run. It has other senses, including carrying out a plan.

example.en: I am going to run the program.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: kernel; core of an operating system
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Kernel is a technical borrowing used in Spanish for the central software that manages hardware and basic system resources.

example.en: The kernel controls memory.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; marks debatirse (‘struggle’)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Debatirse uses se as part of the verb when someone or something struggles against a difficulty. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.es: La empresa se debate entre dos opciones.
example.en: The company struggles between two options.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With se, debate is a present form of debatirse used for one third-person subject. Here it describes effort and difficulty, not a verbal debate.

example.es: El nadador se debate contra la corriente.
example.en: The swimmer struggles against the current.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, an abstraction hides lower-level details behind a simpler interface or layer.

example.es: La biblioteca ofrece una abstracción sencilla.
example.en: The library provides a simple abstraction.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Subyace is the present form of subyacer used with one third-person subject. It often takes a before the thing supported or explained at a deeper level.

example.es: Una regla sencilla subyace al sistema.
example.en: A simple rule underlies the system.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; required after subyacer
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Subyacer a algo places a before the thing that has the deeper basis. Before el, a and el combine as al.

example.en: That idea underlies the project.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a su vez (‘in turn’)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A is fixed at the start of a su vez, an expression that moves to the next linked step or participant.

example.es: Marta avisó a Luis, que a su vez llamó a Ana.
example.en: Marta told Luis, who in turn called Ana.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: its; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Su is the possessive middle word in the fixed expression a su vez. The expression can refer to a person or thing taking its turn in a sequence.

example.es: El segundo equipo, a su vez, revisó los datos.
example.en: The second team, in turn, reviewed the data.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: turn; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Vez ordinarily means a time or occasion. In a su vez, it helps mark the next corresponding step in a chain.

example.es: La lluvia llenó el río, que a su vez inundó el campo.
example.en: The rain filled the river, which in turn flooded the field.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; marks esforzarse (‘make an effort’)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Esforzarse uses se as part of the verb. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.en: She makes an effort to learn.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: With se, esfuerza is the present form of esforzarse used for one third-person subject.

example.en: Tomás makes an effort every day.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, a renderizador turns data or code into the visible image or output shown to a user.

example.en: The renderer creates the image.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Crea is the present form of crear used with one third-person subject or as a familiar positive command.

example.en: The program creates a file.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Objeto can name a physical item or, in computing, a unit of data and behavior.

example.en: The program saves each object.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.es: El vídeo tiene treinta fotogramas por segundo.
example.en: The video has thirty frames per second.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Caerse describes a person or thing losing balance or falling, without naming someone who makes it fall. The attached se changes with the person in changed verb forms: me caigo, te caes, se cae.

example.en: The child may fall.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How does Spanish express thousands of millions of something—what English commonly calls billions?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use miles de millones de, followed by the thing being counted.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Miles and millones stay plural, and de appears both between them and before the counted noun. In standard Spanish numbering, mil millones is one thousand million; English commonly calls that one billion.

example.es: La galaxia contiene miles de millones de estrellas.
example.en: The galaxy contains billions of stars.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: como un loco / como una loca
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something wildly, frantically, or ‘like crazy’ in informal Spanish?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put como un loco after the action for a masculine subject, or como una loca for a feminine subject.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The expression intensifies the manner of an action rather than literally diagnosing anyone. The article and adjective change to una loca for a feminine subject and can become plural for a group.

example.es: Pedro buscó las llaves como un loco.
example.en: Pedro searched for the keys like crazy.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that one idea, cause, or layer underlies something else?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of subyacer, then a, then the thing with that deeper basis.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Subyacer changes for the subject and time; a stays before the thing being supported or explained at a deeper level. A and el combine as al: subyace al problema.

example.es: Una causa común subyace a los dos errores.
example.en: A common cause underlies both errors.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you show that the next person or thing acts ‘in turn’ as part of a chain?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a su vez to introduce the corresponding next step or effect.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The three-word expression stays together. It often follows the person or thing taking the next turn, sometimes between commas, and can connect one cause or layer to the next.

example.es: Ana llamó a Luis, que a su vez avisó a Marta.
example.en: Ana called Luis, who in turn told Marta.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does the long chain of computing layers make the cat-video punchline funny?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: A huge, intricate stack of hardware and software work is reduced to the viewer's simple wish to watch a cat jump into a box and fall.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The chain moves from processor cycles through an operating-system kernel and compatibility layers to a browser, renderer, plug-in object, and video frames. Calling the viewer a god reverses the perspective: these complex layers serve an ordinary human request, even though the human does not directly control their details.

applications.explanationEn: Miles de millones de supplies the large quantity frame, and ciclos names what is being counted.
Para introduces the purpose, and ejecutar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to kernel, and se debate supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Como un loco intensifies the manner of the struggle as frantic rather than describing a literal identity.
The three fixed words introduce movement through the layers that follow.
Para introduces the intended result, and crear stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to sistema, and subyace supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Subyace is the present verb for one underlying system, and a introduces the named system above it.

applications.exampleEs: OS X, QUE A SU VEZ SE ESFUERZA
applications.explanationEn: The excluded product name is the thing being described; que opens the added information, and se esfuerza supplies its verb.
A su vez moves from one software layer to the next corresponding step in the chain.
Para introduces the purpose, and correr stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Que points back to renderizador, and crea supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Que points back to objeto, and muestra supplies the verb at the core of the added information.
Docenas gives the approximate quantity, de links it to what is counted, and fotogramas names those counted images.

applications.explanationEn: Quería changes to express the past desire, while ver stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the desired action.
Quería uses the imperfect because it presents wanting as a past state that supplies background, not as one bounded event.
A marks the specific animate being receiving the seeing action, and un gato names that being.
